# Agentic Pipeline Report: 20 Newsgroups (4 categories)

**Data and cleaning.** I loaded the 20-newsgroups training set with four categories (`load_dataset_1`): 2,257 documents, with 480 alt.atheism, 584 comp.graphics, 594 sci.med and 599 soc.religion.christian. These numbers match the Master notebook. The data has no missing texts (`check_missing_3`) and no duplicate documents (`check_duplicates_4`), so nothing was removed. Document lengths are strongly right-skewed (`describe_data_5`). The median is 1,235 characters, but the maximum is 60,713, a comp.graphics post. soc.religion.christian has the longest median (1,649) and comp.graphics the shortest (883). A random sample of 1,000 documents (`sample_data_6`) contained 206 / 247 / 277 / 270 documents from the four categories. Proportional sampling would give about 213 / 259 / 263 / 265, so the sample keeps the category balance. I used the sample only for this check and ran every later step on the full 2,257 documents.

![Document length by category](../plots/林元鴻_agentic-pipeline_plot_describe_data_5.png)

**Document-term matrix and filtering.** The unigram DTM (`dtm_7`) is 2,257 × 35,788 with 365,886 non-zero cells, a sparsity of 99.547%. Raw frequency is not a useful way to pick features here. Of the top 20 terms (`term_freq_8`), 19 are stop words and the 20th is `edu`, from e-mail addresses. The first 20 columns of the DTM (`dtm_heatmap_9`) are numeric tokens such as `00` and `000`, and the 20 × 20 slice is almost entirely zero. A variance filter with threshold 0.01 (`variance_10`) keeps 5,354 of the 35,788 terms. However, the highest-variance terms are still function words. The top 20 by variance used in `feature_correlation_13` are *the, of, to, and, is, …* plus `jpeg`, and the function words are strongly inter-correlated (e.g. *the*–*of* r = 0.94). `jpeg` is probably driven by a few very long comp.graphics posts. Variance on raw counts mostly measures how long a document is, not what it is about. Note that in my implementation the variance, Pearson and Spearman filters each analyse the full DTM independently; they do not shrink the matrix used by later steps.

![Correlation among the 20 highest-variance terms](../plots/林元鴻_agentic-pipeline_plot_feature_correlation_13.png)

**Correlation with sci.med: an author artifact.** The strongest Pearson correlations with sci.med (`pearson_11`) are *pitt, gordon, geb, banks, n3jxp, intellect, chastity, dsl, shameful, cadre, surrender*. These are not medical words. They come from the e-mail signature of one prolific sci.med poster: Gordon Banks, N3JXP, geb@cs.pitt.edu, with the quote "Skepticism is the chastity of the intellect, and it is shameful to surrender it too soon." Several of these terms have identical r values (e.g. 0.3174 for *intellect* and *chastity*) because they always appear together in that signature. The first genuinely medical term, *medicine*, only appears at rank 12 (r = 0.263). Spearman (`spearman_12`) shares 14 of the top 20 terms but ranks more real topic words highly: *disease* 0.320, *medical* 0.319, *doctor*, *health*, *patients*. It also surfaces a negative term, *god* (−0.319), which marks documents from the two religion groups. The lesson is that correlation-based feature selection rewards whatever co-occurs with the label, including authors and signatures. Headers and signatures should be stripped before selecting features.

![Top 15 Pearson correlations with sci.med](../plots/林元鴻_agentic-pipeline_plot_turn78.png)

**Frequent patterns.** With the `term_frequency` filter and Top-K mining (FAE, k = 20), sci.med (`mine_patterns_14`, 15,170 of 15,964 terms kept) and comp.graphics (`mine_patterns_15`, 12,830 of 13,480 kept) only produce single generic words with support of about 17–23 documents (e.g. *mass, easy, advance*; *recently, personally, rumours*). This filter removes the top 5% most frequent terms per category, and the topic words are among them. Running sci.med again with the `tfidf` filter (`mine_patterns_21`) keeps the frequent terms, but the patterns are then e-mail header fields: {subject} appears in all 594 documents, {lines} in 585, {organization} in 582, {organization, lines, subject, edu} in 400, and {writes} and {article} in about 343. Neither setting yields topical patterns. Mining on this data needs header removal and stop-word filtering first.

**Dimension reduction and similarity.** PCA on the 1,000 highest-variance terms (`reduce_pca_16`) puts 70.5% of the variance on the first component and 4.5% on the second. In the plot, almost all documents bunch near the origin while a handful of very long documents stretch out along component 1. The first component mostly reflects document length, and the categories are not separated. t-SNE with perplexity 30 (`reduce_tsne_17`) spreads the points out, but the four categories remain heavily mixed. There are only partial regions: comp.graphics toward the left, soc.religion.christian toward the right, and one tight sci.med cluster at the bottom. During the run the agent first claimed that t-SNE separates the categories "significantly better" and that the two religion groups overlap most. It had only seen 5 preview coordinates, so I asked it to restate the comparison using only the tool outputs; these observations come from my own reading of the saved plots. The labels were binarized into 4 classes, giving a 2,257 × 4 matrix (`binarize_18`). Finally, cosine similarity between two comp.graphics posts (`cosine_similarity_19`, documents 0 and 1) is 0.353, barely higher than between a comp.graphics and a soc.religion.christian post (`cosine_similarity_20`, documents 0 and 2), which is 0.340. With raw counts, the shared stop words and header lines dominate the vectors.

![PCA](../plots/林元鴻_agentic-pipeline_plot_reduce_pca_16.png)
![t-SNE](../plots/林元鴻_agentic-pipeline_plot_reduce_tsne_17.png)

**Conclusion.** The same problem appears at every stage: on raw newsgroup text, headers (*subject, lines, organization, edu*), stop words, signatures and document length dominate the signal. They decide the top frequencies, the high-variance terms, the strongest correlations, the frequent patterns, the first principal component and the cosine similarities. The pipeline itself works and matches the Master notebook's numbers. To get topic-level structure, the next step would be to remove headers, footers and quotes, filter stop words, and use TF-IDF or length-normalized features before filtering, mining or reducing.
